title: u128::unchecked_sub
text:
# u128::unchecked_sub

Kind: method
Defined in: `u128`
Signature: `pub const unsafe fn unchecked_sub(self, rhs: u128) -> u128`
Stable since: Rust 1.79.0

Unchecked integer subtraction. Computes `self - rhs`, assuming overflow
cannot occur.

Calling `x.unchecked_sub(y)` is semantically equivalent to calling
`x.``checked_sub``(y).``unwrap_unchecked``()`.

If you're just trying to avoid the panic in debug mode, then **do not**
use this.  Instead, you're looking for `wrapping_sub`.

If you find yourself writing code like this:

```rust
if foo >= bar {
    // SAFETY: just checked it will not overflow
    let diff = unsafe { foo.unchecked_sub(bar) };
    // ... use diff ...
}
```

Consider changing it to

```rust
if let Some(diff) = foo.checked_sub(bar) {
    // ... use diff ...
}
```

As that does exactly the same thing -- including telling the optimizer
that the subtraction cannot overflow -- but avoids needing `unsafe`.

# Safety

This results in undefined behavior when overflow occurs, i.e. when
`checked_sub` would return `None`.

text:
# u128::wrapping_neg

Kind: method
Defined in: `u128`
Signature: `pub const fn wrapping_neg(self) -> u128`
Stable since: Rust 1.2.0

Wrapping (modular) negation. Computes `-self`,
wrapping around at the boundary of the type.

Since unsigned types do not have negative equivalents
all applications of this function will wrap (except for `-0`).
For values smaller than the corresponding signed type's maximum
the result is the same as casting the corresponding signed value.
Any larger values are equivalent to `MAX + 1 - (val - MAX - 1)` where
`MAX` is the corresponding signed type's maximum.

# Examples

```rust
assert_eq!(0_u128.wrapping_neg(), 0);
assert_eq!(u128::MAX.wrapping_neg(), 1);
assert_eq!(13_u128.wrapping_neg(), (!13) + 1);
assert_eq!(42_u128.wrapping_neg(), !(42 - 1));
```

title: u128::wrapping_shl
text:
# u128::wrapping_shl

Kind: method
Defined in: `u128`
Signature: `pub const fn wrapping_shl(self, rhs: u32) -> u128`
Stable since: Rust 1.2.0

Panic-free bitwise shift-left; yields `self << mask(rhs)`,
where `mask` removes any high-order bits of `rhs` that
would cause the shift to exceed the bitwidth of the type.

Beware that, unlike most other `wrapping_*` methods on integers, this
does *not* give the same result as doing the shift in infinite precision
then truncating as needed. Instead, the behaviour of this method matches what shift instructions
do on many processors, and is what the `<<` operator does when overflow
checks are disabled, but numerically it's weird.  Consider, instead,
using `Self::unbounded_shl` which has nicer behaviour.

Note that this is *not* the same as a rotate-left; the
RHS of a wrapping shift-left is restricted to the range
of the type, rather than the bits shifted out of the LHS
being returned to the other end. The primitive integer
types all implement a `rotate_left` function,
which may be what you want instead.

# Examples

```rust
assert_eq!(1_u128.wrapping_shl(7), 128);
assert_eq!(0b101_u128.wrapping_shl(0), 0b101);
assert_eq!(0b101_u128.wrapping_shl(1), 0b1010);
assert_eq!(0b101_u128.wrapping_shl(2), 0b10100);
assert_eq!(u128::MAX.wrapping_shl(2), u128::MAX - 3);
assert_eq!(42_u128.wrapping_shl(128), 42);
assert_eq!(42_u128.wrapping_shl(1).wrapping_shl(127), 0);
assert_eq!(1_u128.wrapping_shl(128), 1);
assert_eq!(5_u128.wrapping_shl(1025), 10);
```

title: u128::wrapping_shr
text:
# u128::wrapping_shr

Kind: method
Defined in: `u128`
Signature: `pub const fn wrapping_shr(self, rhs: u32) -> u128`
Stable since: Rust 1.2.0

Panic-free bitwise shift-right; yields `self >> mask(rhs)`,
where `mask` removes any high-order bits of `rhs` that
would cause the shift to exceed the bitwidth of the type.

Beware that, unlike most other `wrapping_*` methods on integers, this
does *not* give the same result as doing the shift in infinite precision
then truncating as needed. Instead, the behaviour of this method matches what shift instructions
do on many processors, and is what the `>>` operator does when overflow
checks are disabled, but numerically it's weird.  Consider, instead,
using `Self::unbounded_shr` which has nicer behaviour.

Note that this is *not* the same as a rotate-right; the
RHS of a wrapping shift-right is restricted to the range
of the type, rather than the bits shifted out of the LHS
being returned to the other end. The primitive integer
types all implement a `rotate_right` function,
which may be what you want instead.

# Examples

```rust
assert_eq!(128_u128.wrapping_shr(7), 1);
assert_eq!(0b1010_u128.wrapping_shr(0), 0b1010);
assert_eq!(0b1010_u128.wrapping_shr(1), 0b101);
assert_eq!(0b1010_u128.wrapping_shr(2), 0b10);
assert_eq!(u128::MAX.wrapping_shr(1), i128::MAX.cast_unsigned());
assert_eq!(42_u128.wrapping_shr(128), 42);
assert_eq!(42_u128.wrapping_shr(1).wrapping_shr(127), 0);
assert_eq!(128_u128.wrapping_shr(128), 128);
assert_eq!(10_u128.wrapping_shr(1025), 5);
```

# u16::from_str_radix

Kind: method
Defined in: `u16`
Signature: `pub const fn from_str_radix(src: &str, radix: u32) -> Result<u16, ParseIntError>`
Stable since: Rust 1.0.0

Parses an integer from a string slice with digits in a given base.

The string is expected to be an optional
 `+` 
sign followed by only digits. Leading and trailing non-digit characters (including
whitespace) represent an error. Underscores (which are accepted in Rust literals)
also represent an error.

Digits are a subset of these characters, depending on `radix`:
* `0-9`
* `a-z`
* `A-Z`

# Panics

This function panics if `radix` is not in the range from 2 to 36.

# See also
If the string to be parsed is in base 10 (decimal),
`from_str` or `str::parse` can also be used.

# Examples

```rust
assert_eq!(u16::from_str_radix("A", 16), Ok(10));
```
Trailing space returns error:

Kind: method

Signature: `pub const fn midpoint(self, rhs: u16) -> u16`
Stable since: Rust 1.85.0

Calculates the midpoint (average) between `self` and `rhs`.

# u16::next_multiple_of

Kind: method
Defined in: `u16`
Signature: `pub const fn next_multiple_of(self, rhs: u16) -> u16`
Stable since: Rust 1.73.0

Calculates the smallest value greater than or equal to `self` that
is a multiple of `rhs`.

# Panics

This function will panic if `rhs` is zero.

## Overflow behavior

On overflow, this function will panic if overflow checks are enabled (default in debug
mode) and wrap if overflow checks are disabled (default in release mode).

# Examples

```rust
assert_eq!(16_u16.next_multiple_of(8), 16);
assert_eq!(23_u16.next_multiple_of(8), 24);
```

Defined in: `u16`
Signature: `pub const fn next_power_of_two(self) -> u16`
Stable since: Rust 1.0.0

Returns the smallest power of two greater than or equal to `self`.

When return value overflows (i.e., `self > (1 << (N-1))` for type
`uN`), it panics in debug mode and the return value is wrapped to 0 in
release mode (the only situation in which this method can return 0).

# Examples

```rust
assert_eq!(2u16.next_power_of_two(), 2);
assert_eq!(3u16.next_power_of_two(), 4);
assert_eq!(0u16.next_power_of_two(), 1);
```

Stable since: Rust 1.38.0

Calculates the quotient of Euclidean division `self.div_euclid(rhs)`.

Returns a tuple of the divisor along with a boolean indicating
whether an arithmetic overflow would occur. Note that for unsigned
integers overflow never occurs, so the second value is always

Since, for the positive integers, all common
definitions of division are equal, this
is exactly equal to `self.overflowing_div(rhs)`.

# u16::overflowing_mul

Kind: method
Defined in: `u16`
Signature: `pub const fn overflowing_mul(self, rhs: u16) -> (u16, bool)`
Stable since: Rust 1.7.0

Calculates the multiplication of `self` and `rhs`.

Returns a tuple of the multiplication along with a boolean
indicating whether an arithmetic overflow would occur. If an
overflow would have occurred then the wrapped value is returned.

If you want the *value* of the overflow, rather than just *whether*
an overflow occurred, see `Self::carrying_mul`.

# Examples

Please note that this example is shared among integer types, which is why `u32` is used.

```rust
assert_eq!(5u32.overflowing_mul(2), (10, false));
assert_eq!(1_000_000_000u32.overflowing_mul(10), (1410065408, true));
```

not overflow.

# u16::overflowing_shl

Kind: method
Defined in: `u16`
Signature: `pub const fn overflowing_shl(self, rhs: u32) -> (u16, bool)`
Stable since: Rust 1.7.0

Shifts self left by `rhs` bits.

Returns a tuple of the shifted version of self along with a boolean
indicating whether the shift value was larger than or equal to the
number of bits. If the shift value is too large, then value is
masked (N-1) where N is the number of bits, and this value is then
used to perform the shift.

# Examples

```rust
assert_eq!(0x1u16.overflowing_shl(4), (0x10, false));
assert_eq!(0x1u16.overflowing_shl(132), (0x10, true));
assert_eq!(0x10u16.overflowing_shl(15), (0, false));
```

title: u16::rotate_left
text:
# u16::rotate_left

Kind: method
Defined in: `u16`
Signature: `pub const fn rotate_left(self, n: u32) -> u16`
Stable since: Rust 1.0.0

Shifts the bits to the left by a specified amount, `n`,
wrapping the truncated bits to the end of the resulting integer.

`rotate_left(n)` is equivalent to applying `rotate_left(1)` a total of `n` times. In
particular, a rotation by the number of bits in `self` returns the input value
unchanged.

Please note this isn't the same operation as the `<<` shifting operator!

# Examples

```rust
let n = 0xa003u16;
let m = 0x003a;

assert_eq!(n.rotate_left(4), m);
assert_eq!(n.rotate_left(1024), n);
```

`rotate_right(n)` is equivalent to applying `rotate_right(1)` a total of `n` times. In

Stable since: Rust 1.91.0

if overflow occurred.

This function will always panic on overflow, regardless of whether overflow checks are enabled.

# Examples


title: u16::strict_div
text:
# u16::strict_div

Kind: method
Defined in: `u16`
Signature: `pub const fn strict_div(self, rhs: u16) -> u16`
Stable since: Rust 1.91.0

Strict integer division. Computes `self / rhs`.

Strict division on unsigned types is just normal division. There's no
way overflow could ever happen. This function exists so that all
operations are accounted for in the strict operations.

# Panics

This function will panic if `rhs` is zero.

# Examples

```rust
assert_eq!(100u16.strict_div(10), 10);
```

The following panics because of division by zero:

```rust
let _ = (1u16).strict_div(0);
```

Stable since: Rust 1.91.0

Strict Euclidean division. Computes `self.div_euclid(rhs)`.

Strict division on unsigned types is just normal division. There's no
way overflow could ever happen. This function exists so that all
operations are accounted for in the strict operations. Since, for the
positive integers, all common definitions of division are equal, this
is exactly equal to `self.strict_div(rhs)`.

# Panics

This function will panic if `rhs` is zero.

# u16::to_be

Kind: method

Signature: `pub const fn to_be(self) -> u16`

title: u16::unchecked_sub
text:
# u16::unchecked_sub

Kind: method
Defined in: `u16`
Signature: `pub const unsafe fn unchecked_sub(self, rhs: u16) -> u16`
Stable since: Rust 1.79.0

Unchecked integer subtraction. Computes `self - rhs`, assuming overflow
cannot occur.

Calling `x.unchecked_sub(y)` is semantically equivalent to calling
`x.``checked_sub``(y).``unwrap_unchecked``()`.

If you're just trying to avoid the panic in debug mode, then **do not**
use this.  Instead, you're looking for `wrapping_sub`.

If you find yourself writing code like this:

```rust
if foo >= bar {
    // SAFETY: just checked it will not overflow
    let diff = unsafe { foo.unchecked_sub(bar) };
    // ... use diff ...
}
```

Consider changing it to

```rust
if let Some(diff) = foo.checked_sub(bar) {
    // ... use diff ...
}
```

As that does exactly the same thing -- including telling the optimizer
that the subtraction cannot overflow -- but avoids needing `unsafe`.

# Safety

This results in undefined behavior when overflow occurs, i.e. when
`checked_sub` would return `None`.

title: u16::wrapping_neg
text:
# u16::wrapping_neg

Kind: method
Defined in: `u16`
Signature: `pub const fn wrapping_neg(self) -> u16`
Stable since: Rust 1.2.0

Wrapping (modular) negation. Computes `-self`,
wrapping around at the boundary of the type.

Since unsigned types do not have negative equivalents
all applications of this function will wrap (except for `-0`).
For values smaller than the corresponding signed type's maximum
the result is the same as casting the corresponding signed value.
Any larger values are equivalent to `MAX + 1 - (val - MAX - 1)` where
`MAX` is the corresponding signed type's maximum.

# Examples

```rust
assert_eq!(0_u16.wrapping_neg(), 0);
assert_eq!(u16::MAX.wrapping_neg(), 1);
assert_eq!(13_u16.wrapping_neg(), (!13) + 1);
assert_eq!(42_u16.wrapping_neg(), !(42 - 1));
```

title: u16::wrapping_shl
text:
# u16::wrapping_shl

Kind: method
Defined in: `u16`
Signature: `pub const fn wrapping_shl(self, rhs: u32) -> u16`
Stable since: Rust 1.2.0

Panic-free bitwise shift-left; yields `self << mask(rhs)`,
where `mask` removes any high-order bits of `rhs` that
would cause the shift to exceed the bitwidth of the type.

Beware that, unlike most other `wrapping_*` methods on integers, this
does *not* give the same result as doing the shift in infinite precision
then truncating as needed. Instead, the behaviour of this method matches what shift instructions
do on many processors, and is what the `<<` operator does when overflow
checks are disabled, but numerically it's weird.  Consider, instead,
using `Self::unbounded_shl` which has nicer behaviour.

Note that this is *not* the same as a rotate-left; the
RHS of a wrapping shift-left is restricted to the range
of the type, rather than the bits shifted out of the LHS
being returned to the other end. The primitive integer
types all implement a `rotate_left` function,
which may be what you want instead.

# Examples

```rust
assert_eq!(1_u16.wrapping_shl(7), 128);
assert_eq!(0b101_u16.wrapping_shl(0), 0b101);
assert_eq!(0b101_u16.wrapping_shl(1), 0b1010);
assert_eq!(0b101_u16.wrapping_shl(2), 0b10100);
assert_eq!(u16::MAX.wrapping_shl(2), u16::MAX - 3);
assert_eq!(42_u16.wrapping_shl(16), 42);
assert_eq!(42_u16.wrapping_shl(1).wrapping_shl(15), 0);
assert_eq!(1_u16.wrapping_shl(128), 1);
assert_eq!(5_u16.wrapping_shl(1025), 10);
```

title: u16::wrapping_shr
text:
# u16::wrapping_shr

Kind: method
Defined in: `u16`
Signature: `pub const fn wrapping_shr(self, rhs: u32) -> u16`
Stable since: Rust 1.2.0

Panic-free bitwise shift-right; yields `self >> mask(rhs)`,
where `mask` removes any high-order bits of `rhs` that
would cause the shift to exceed the bitwidth of the type.

Beware that, unlike most other `wrapping_*` methods on integers, this
does *not* give the same result as doing the shift in infinite precision
then truncating as needed. Instead, the behaviour of this method matches what shift instructions
do on many processors, and is what the `>>` operator does when overflow
checks are disabled, but numerically it's weird.  Consider, instead,
using `Self::unbounded_shr` which has nicer behaviour.

Note that this is *not* the same as a rotate-right; the
RHS of a wrapping shift-right is restricted to the range
of the type, rather than the bits shifted out of the LHS
being returned to the other end. The primitive integer
types all implement a `rotate_right` function,
which may be what you want instead.

# Examples

```rust
assert_eq!(128_u16.wrapping_shr(7), 1);
assert_eq!(0b1010_u16.wrapping_shr(0), 0b1010);
assert_eq!(0b1010_u16.wrapping_shr(1), 0b101);
assert_eq!(0b1010_u16.wrapping_shr(2), 0b10);
assert_eq!(u16::MAX.wrapping_shr(1), i16::MAX.cast_unsigned());
assert_eq!(42_u16.wrapping_shr(16), 42);
assert_eq!(42_u16.wrapping_shr(1).wrapping_shr(15), 0);
assert_eq!(128_u16.wrapping_shr(128), 128);
assert_eq!(10_u16.wrapping_shr(1025), 5);
```

# u32::from_be

Kind: method
Defined in: `u32`
Signature: `pub const fn from_be(x: u32) -> u32`
Stable since: Rust 1.0.0

Converts an integer from big endian to the target's endianness.

On big endian this is a no-op. On little endian the bytes are
swapped.

# Examples

```rust
let n = 0x1Au32;

if cfg!(target_endian = "big") {
    assert_eq!(u32::from_be(n), n)
} else {
    assert_eq!(u32::from_be(n), n.swap_bytes())
}
```

text:
# u32::from_str_radix

Kind: method
Defined in: `u32`
Signature: `pub const fn from_str_radix(src: &str, radix: u32) -> Result<u32, ParseIntError>`
Stable since: Rust 1.0.0

Parses an integer from a string slice with digits in a given base.

The string is expected to be an optional
 `+` 
sign followed by only digits. Leading and trailing non-digit characters (including
whitespace) represent an error. Underscores (which are accepted in Rust literals)
also represent an error.

Digits are a subset of these characters, depending on `radix`:
* `0-9`
* `a-z`
* `A-Z`

# Panics

This function panics if `radix` is not in the range from 2 to 36.

# See also
If the string to be parsed is in base 10 (decimal),
`from_str` or `str::parse` can also be used.

# Examples

```rust
assert_eq!(u32::from_str_radix("A", 16), Ok(10));
```
Trailing space returns error:
```rust
assert!(u32::from_str_radix("1 ", 10).is_err());
```

title: u32::midpoint
text:
# u32::midpoint

Kind: method
Defined in: `u32`
Signature: `pub const fn midpoint(self, rhs: u32) -> u32`
Stable since: Rust 1.85.0

Calculates the midpoint (average) between `self` and `rhs`.

`midpoint(a, b)` is `(a + b) / 2` as if it were performed in a
sufficiently-large unsigned integral type. This implies that the result is
always rounded towards zero and that no overflow will ever occur.

# Examples

```rust
assert_eq!(0u32.midpoint(4), 2);
assert_eq!(1u32.midpoint(4), 2);
```

title: u32::next_multiple_of
text:
# u32::next_multiple_of

Kind: method
Defined in: `u32`
Signature: `pub const fn next_multiple_of(self, rhs: u32) -> u32`
Stable since: Rust 1.73.0

Calculates the smallest value greater than or equal to `self` that
is a multiple of `rhs`.

# Panics

This function will panic if `rhs` is zero.

## Overflow behavior

On overflow, this function will panic if overflow checks are enabled (default in debug
mode) and wrap if overflow checks are disabled (default in release mode).

# Examples

```rust
assert_eq!(16_u32.next_multiple_of(8), 16);
assert_eq!(23_u32.next_multiple_of(8), 24);
```

title: u32::next_power_of_two
text:
# u32::next_power_of_two

Kind: method
Defined in: `u32`
Signature: `pub const fn next_power_of_two(self) -> u32`
Stable since: Rust 1.0.0

Returns the smallest power of two greater than or equal to `self`.

When return value overflows (i.e., `self > (1 << (N-1))` for type
`uN`), it panics in debug mode and the return value is wrapped to 0 in
release mode (the only situation in which this method can return 0).

# Examples

```rust
assert_eq!(2u32.next_power_of_two(), 2);
assert_eq!(3u32.next_power_of_two(), 4);
assert_eq!(0u32.next_power_of_two(), 1);
```

overflow would have occurred then the wrapped value is returned.

If you want the *value* of the overflow, rather than just *whether*

Please note that this example is shared among integer types, which is why `u32` is used.

# u32::overflowing_shl

Kind: method
Defined in: `u32`
Signature: `pub const fn overflowing_shl(self, rhs: u32) -> (u32, bool)`
Stable since: Rust 1.7.0

Shifts self left by `rhs` bits.

Returns a tuple of the shifted version of self along with a boolean
indicating whether the shift value was larger than or equal to the
number of bits. If the shift value is too large, then value is
masked (N-1) where N is the number of bits, and this value is then
used to perform the shift.

# Examples

```rust
assert_eq!(0x1u32.overflowing_shl(4), (0x10, false));
assert_eq!(0x1u32.overflowing_shl(132), (0x10, true));
assert_eq!(0x10u32.overflowing_shl(31), (0, false));
```

                second least-significant bit becomes second most-significant bit, etc.

title: u32::rotate_left
text:
# u32::rotate_left

Kind: method
Defined in: `u32`
Signature: `pub const fn rotate_left(self, n: u32) -> u32`
Stable since: Rust 1.0.0

Shifts the bits to the left by a specified amount, `n`,
wrapping the truncated bits to the end of the resulting integer.

`rotate_left(n)` is equivalent to applying `rotate_left(1)` a total of `n` times. In
particular, a rotation by the number of bits in `self` returns the input value
unchanged.

Please note this isn't the same operation as the `<<` shifting operator!

# Examples

```rust
let n = 0x010000b3u32;
let m = 0x0000b301;

assert_eq!(n.rotate_left(8), m);
assert_eq!(n.rotate_left(1024), n);
```

Kind: method
Defined in: `u32`
Signature: `pub const fn rotate_right(self, n: u32) -> u32`
Stable since: Rust 1.0.0

Shifts the bits to the right by a specified amount, `n`,
wrapping the truncated bits to the beginning of the resulting
integer.

`rotate_right(n)` is equivalent to applying `rotate_right(1)` a total of `n` times. In
particular, a rotation by the number of bits in `self` returns the input value
unchanged.

Please note this isn't the same operation as the `>>` shifting operator!

# Examples

```rust
let n = 0x0000b301u32;
let m = 0x010000b3;

assert_eq!(n.rotate_right(8), m);
assert_eq!(n.rotate_right(1024), n);
```

Kind: method
Defined in: `u32`

Stable since: Rust 1.91.0

Strict integer addition. Computes `self + rhs`, panicking

Signature: `pub const fn strict_shr(self, rhs: u32) -> u32`
Stable since: Rust 1.91.0

Strict shift right. Computes `self >> rhs`, panicking if `rhs` is
larger than or equal to the number of bits in `self`.

# Panics

## Overflow behavior

This function will always panic on overflow, regardless of whether overflow checks are enabled.

# Examples

```rust
assert_eq!(0x10u32.strict_shr(4), 0x1);
```

The following panics because of overflow:

```rust
let _ = 0x10u32.strict_shr(129);
```

# u32::to_be

Kind: method
Defined in: `u32`
Signature: `pub const fn to_be(self) -> u32`
Stable since: Rust 1.0.0

Converts `self` to big endian from the target's endianness.

On big endian this is a no-op. On little endian the bytes are
swapped.

# Examples

```rust
let n = 0x1Au32;

if cfg!(target_endian = "big") {
    assert_eq!(n.to_be(), n)
} else {
    assert_eq!(n.to_be(), n.swap_bytes())
}
```

title: u32::unchecked_sub

# u32::unchecked_sub

Kind: method
Defined in: `u32`
Signature: `pub const unsafe fn unchecked_sub(self, rhs: u32) -> u32`
Stable since: Rust 1.79.0

Unchecked integer subtraction. Computes `self - rhs`, assuming overflow
cannot occur.

Calling `x.unchecked_sub(y)` is semantically equivalent to calling
`x.``checked_sub``(y).``unwrap_unchecked``()`.

If you're just trying to avoid the panic in debug mode, then **do not**
use this.  Instead, you're looking for `wrapping_sub`.

If you find yourself writing code like this:

```rust
if foo >= bar {
    // SAFETY: just checked it will not overflow
    let diff = unsafe { foo.unchecked_sub(bar) };
    // ... use diff ...
}
```

Consider changing it to

```rust
if let Some(diff) = foo.checked_sub(bar) {
    // ... use diff ...
}
```

As that does exactly the same thing -- including telling the optimizer
that the subtraction cannot overflow -- but avoids needing `unsafe`.

# Safety

This results in undefined behavior when overflow occurs, i.e. when
`checked_sub` would return `None`.

title: u32::wrapping_neg
text:
# u32::wrapping_neg

Kind: method
Defined in: `u32`
Signature: `pub const fn wrapping_neg(self) -> u32`
Stable since: Rust 1.2.0

Wrapping (modular) negation. Computes `-self`,
wrapping around at the boundary of the type.

Since unsigned types do not have negative equivalents
all applications of this function will wrap (except for `-0`).
For values smaller than the corresponding signed type's maximum
the result is the same as casting the corresponding signed value.
Any larger values are equivalent to `MAX + 1 - (val - MAX - 1)` where
`MAX` is the corresponding signed type's maximum.

# Examples

```rust
assert_eq!(0_u32.wrapping_neg(), 0);
assert_eq!(u32::MAX.wrapping_neg(), 1);
assert_eq!(13_u32.wrapping_neg(), (!13) + 1);
assert_eq!(42_u32.wrapping_neg(), !(42 - 1));
```

title: u32::wrapping_shl
text:
# u32::wrapping_shl

Kind: method
Defined in: `u32`
Signature: `pub const fn wrapping_shl(self, rhs: u32) -> u32`
Stable since: Rust 1.2.0

Panic-free bitwise shift-left; yields `self << mask(rhs)`,
where `mask` removes any high-order bits of `rhs` that
would cause the shift to exceed the bitwidth of the type.

Beware that, unlike most other `wrapping_*` methods on integers, this
does *not* give the same result as doing the shift in infinite precision
then truncating as needed. Instead, the behaviour of this method matches what shift instructions
do on many processors, and is what the `<<` operator does when overflow
checks are disabled, but numerically it's weird.  Consider, instead,
using `Self::unbounded_shl` which has nicer behaviour.

Note that this is *not* the same as a rotate-left; the
RHS of a wrapping shift-left is restricted to the range
of the type, rather than the bits shifted out of the LHS
being returned to the other end. The primitive integer
types all implement a `rotate_left` function,
which may be what you want instead.

# Examples

```rust
assert_eq!(1_u32.wrapping_shl(7), 128);
assert_eq!(0b101_u32.wrapping_shl(0), 0b101);
assert_eq!(0b101_u32.wrapping_shl(1), 0b1010);
assert_eq!(0b101_u32.wrapping_shl(2), 0b10100);
assert_eq!(u32::MAX.wrapping_shl(2), u32::MAX - 3);
assert_eq!(42_u32.wrapping_shl(32), 42);
assert_eq!(42_u32.wrapping_shl(1).wrapping_shl(31), 0);
assert_eq!(1_u32.wrapping_shl(128), 1);
assert_eq!(5_u32.wrapping_shl(1025), 10);
```

title: u32::wrapping_shr
text:
# u32::wrapping_shr

Kind: method
Defined in: `u32`
Signature: `pub const fn wrapping_shr(self, rhs: u32) -> u32`
Stable since: Rust 1.2.0

Panic-free bitwise shift-right; yields `self >> mask(rhs)`,
where `mask` removes any high-order bits of `rhs` that
would cause the shift to exceed the bitwidth of the type.

Beware that, unlike most other `wrapping_*` methods on integers, this
does *not* give the same result as doing the shift in infinite precision
then truncating as needed. Instead, the behaviour of this method matches what shift instructions
do on many processors, and is what the `>>` operator does when overflow
checks are disabled, but numerically it's weird.  Consider, instead,
using `Self::unbounded_shr` which has nicer behaviour.

Note that this is *not* the same as a rotate-right; the
RHS of a wrapping shift-right is restricted to the range
of the type, rather than the bits shifted out of the LHS
being returned to the other end. The primitive integer
types all implement a `rotate_right` function,
which may be what you want instead.

# Examples

```rust
assert_eq!(128_u32.wrapping_shr(7), 1);
assert_eq!(0b1010_u32.wrapping_shr(0), 0b1010);
assert_eq!(0b1010_u32.wrapping_shr(1), 0b101);
assert_eq!(0b1010_u32.wrapping_shr(2), 0b10);
assert_eq!(u32::MAX.wrapping_shr(1), i32::MAX.cast_unsigned());
assert_eq!(42_u32.wrapping_shr(32), 42);
assert_eq!(42_u32.wrapping_shr(1).wrapping_shr(31), 0);
assert_eq!(128_u32.wrapping_shr(128), 128);
assert_eq!(10_u32.wrapping_shr(1025), 5);
```

# u64::from_be

Kind: method
Defined in: `u64`
Signature: `pub const fn from_be(x: u64) -> u64`
Stable since: Rust 1.0.0

Converts an integer from big endian to the target's endianness.

On big endian this is a no-op. On little endian the bytes are
swapped.

# Examples

```rust
let n = 0x1Au64;

if cfg!(target_endian = "big") {
    assert_eq!(u64::from_be(n), n)
} else {
    assert_eq!(u64::from_be(n), n.swap_bytes())
}
```

text:
# u64::from_str_radix

Kind: method
Defined in: `u64`
Signature: `pub const fn from_str_radix(src: &str, radix: u32) -> Result<u64, ParseIntError>`
Stable since: Rust 1.0.0

Parses an integer from a string slice with digits in a given base.

The string is expected to be an optional
 `+` 
sign followed by only digits. Leading and trailing non-digit characters (including
whitespace) represent an error. Underscores (which are accepted in Rust literals)
also represent an error.

Digits are a subset of these characters, depending on `radix`:
* `0-9`
* `a-z`
* `A-Z`

# Panics

This function panics if `radix` is not in the range from 2 to 36.

# See also
If the string to be parsed is in base 10 (decimal),
`from_str` or `str::parse` can also be used.

# Examples

```rust
assert_eq!(u64::from_str_radix("A", 16), Ok(10));
```
Trailing space returns error:
```rust
assert!(u64::from_str_radix("1 ", 10).is_err());
```

Calculates the smallest value greater than or equal to `self` that
is a multiple of `rhs`.

# Panics

This function will panic if `rhs` is zero.

## Overflow behavior

On overflow, this function will panic if overflow checks are enabled (default in debug
mode) and wrap if overflow checks are disabled (default in release mode).


When return value overflows (i.e., `self > (1 << (N-1))` for type

release mode (the only situation in which this method can return 0).

# Examples

```rust
assert_eq!(2u64.next_power_of_two(), 2);
assert_eq!(3u64.next_power_of_two(), 4);
```

Shifts self left by `rhs` bits.

Returns a tuple of the shifted version of self along with a boolean

title: u64::rotate_left
text:
# u64::rotate_left

Kind: method
Defined in: `u64`
Signature: `pub const fn rotate_left(self, n: u32) -> u64`
Stable since: Rust 1.0.0

Shifts the bits to the left by a specified amount, `n`,
wrapping the truncated bits to the end of the resulting integer.

`rotate_left(n)` is equivalent to applying `rotate_left(1)` a total of `n` times. In
particular, a rotation by the number of bits in `self` returns the input value
unchanged.

Please note this isn't the same operation as the `<<` shifting operator!

# Examples

```rust
let n = 0x0aa00000000006e1u64;
let m = 0x00000000006e10aa;

assert_eq!(n.rotate_left(12), m);
assert_eq!(n.rotate_left(1024), n);
```

title: u64::rotate_right
text:
# u64::rotate_right

Kind: method
Defined in: `u64`
Signature: `pub const fn rotate_right(self, n: u32) -> u64`
Stable since: Rust 1.0.0

Shifts the bits to the right by a specified amount, `n`,
wrapping the truncated bits to the beginning of the resulting
integer.

`rotate_right(n)` is equivalent to applying `rotate_right(1)` a total of `n` times. In
particular, a rotation by the number of bits in `self` returns the input value
unchanged.

Please note this isn't the same operation as the `>>` shifting operator!

# Examples

```rust
let n = 0x00000000006e10aau64;
let m = 0x0aa00000000006e1;

assert_eq!(n.rotate_right(12), m);
assert_eq!(n.rotate_right(1024), n);
```

# u64::to_le_bytes

Kind: method
Defined in: `u64`
Signature: `pub const fn to_le_bytes(self) -> [u8; 8]`
Stable since: Rust 1.32.0

Returns the memory representation of this integer as a byte array in
little-endian byte order.

# Examples

```rust
let bytes = 0x1234567890123456u64.to_le_bytes();
assert_eq!(bytes, [0x56, 0x34, 0x12, 0x90, 0x78, 0x56, 0x34, 0x12]);
```

# u64::unchecked_add

Kind: method
Defined in: `u64`
Signature: `pub const unsafe fn unchecked_add(self, rhs: u64) -> u64`
Stable since: Rust 1.79.0

Unchecked integer addition. Computes `self + rhs`, assuming overflow
cannot occur.

Calling `x.unchecked_add(y)` is semantically equivalent to calling
`x.``checked_add``(y).``unwrap_unchecked``()`.

If you're just trying to avoid the panic in debug mode, then **do not**
use this.  Instead, you're looking for `wrapping_add`.

# Safety

This results in undefined behavior when overflow occurs, i.e. when
`checked_add` would return `None`.

title: u64::unchecked_sub
text:
# u64::unchecked_sub

Kind: method
Defined in: `u64`
Signature: `pub const unsafe fn unchecked_sub(self, rhs: u64) -> u64`
Stable since: Rust 1.79.0

Unchecked integer subtraction. Computes `self - rhs`, assuming overflow
cannot occur.

Calling `x.unchecked_sub(y)` is semantically equivalent to calling
`x.``checked_sub``(y).``unwrap_unchecked``()`.

If you're just trying to avoid the panic in debug mode, then **do not**
use this.  Instead, you're looking for `wrapping_sub`.

If you find yourself writing code like this:

```rust
if foo >= bar {
    // SAFETY: just checked it will not overflow
    let diff = unsafe { foo.unchecked_sub(bar) };
    // ... use diff ...
}
```

Consider changing it to

```rust
if let Some(diff) = foo.checked_sub(bar) {
    // ... use diff ...
}
```

As that does exactly the same thing -- including telling the optimizer
that the subtraction cannot overflow -- but avoids needing `unsafe`.

# Safety

This results in undefined behavior when overflow occurs, i.e. when
`checked_sub` would return `None`.

# u64::wrapping_div

Kind: method
Defined in: `u64`
Signature: `pub const fn wrapping_div(self, rhs: u64) -> u64`
Stable since: Rust 1.2.0

Wrapping (modular) division. Computes `self / rhs`.

Wrapped division on unsigned types is just normal division. There's
no way wrapping could ever happen. This function exists so that all
operations are accounted for in the wrapping operations.

# Panics

This function will panic if `rhs` is zero.

# Examples

```rust
assert_eq!(100u64.wrapping_div(10), 10);
```

Kind: method
Defined in: `u64`
Signature: `pub const fn wrapping_div_euclid(self, rhs: u64) -> u64`
Stable since: Rust 1.38.0

Wrapping Euclidean division. Computes `self.div_euclid(rhs)`.

Wrapped division on unsigned types is just normal division. There's
no way wrapping could ever happen. This function exists so that all
operations are accounted for in the wrapping operations. Since, for
the positive integers, all common definitions of division are equal,
this is exactly equal to `self.wrapping_div(rhs)`.

# Panics

This function will panic if `rhs` is zero.

# Examples

```rust
assert_eq!(100u64.wrapping_div_euclid(10), 10);
```

title: u64::wrapping_neg
text:
# u64::wrapping_neg

Kind: method
Defined in: `u64`
Signature: `pub const fn wrapping_neg(self) -> u64`
Stable since: Rust 1.2.0

Wrapping (modular) negation. Computes `-self`,
wrapping around at the boundary of the type.

Since unsigned types do not have negative equivalents
all applications of this function will wrap (except for `-0`).
For values smaller than the corresponding signed type's maximum
the result is the same as casting the corresponding signed value.
Any larger values are equivalent to `MAX + 1 - (val - MAX - 1)` where
`MAX` is the corresponding signed type's maximum.

# Examples

```rust
assert_eq!(0_u64.wrapping_neg(), 0);
assert_eq!(u64::MAX.wrapping_neg(), 1);
assert_eq!(13_u64.wrapping_neg(), (!13) + 1);
assert_eq!(42_u64.wrapping_neg(), !(42 - 1));
```

title: u64::wrapping_shl
text:
# u64::wrapping_shl

Kind: method
Defined in: `u64`
Signature: `pub const fn wrapping_shl(self, rhs: u32) -> u64`
Stable since: Rust 1.2.0

Panic-free bitwise shift-left; yields `self << mask(rhs)`,
where `mask` removes any high-order bits of `rhs` that
would cause the shift to exceed the bitwidth of the type.

Beware that, unlike most other `wrapping_*` methods on integers, this
does *not* give the same result as doing the shift in infinite precision
then truncating as needed. Instead, the behaviour of this method matches what shift instructions
do on many processors, and is what the `<<` operator does when overflow
checks are disabled, but numerically it's weird.  Consider, instead,
using `Self::unbounded_shl` which has nicer behaviour.

Note that this is *not* the same as a rotate-left; the
RHS of a wrapping shift-left is restricted to the range
of the type, rather than the bits shifted out of the LHS
being returned to the other end. The primitive integer
types all implement a `rotate_left` function,
which may be what you want instead.

# Examples

```rust
assert_eq!(1_u64.wrapping_shl(7), 128);
assert_eq!(0b101_u64.wrapping_shl(0), 0b101);
assert_eq!(0b101_u64.wrapping_shl(1), 0b1010);
assert_eq!(0b101_u64.wrapping_shl(2), 0b10100);
assert_eq!(u64::MAX.wrapping_shl(2), u64::MAX - 3);
assert_eq!(42_u64.wrapping_shl(64), 42);
assert_eq!(42_u64.wrapping_shl(1).wrapping_shl(63), 0);
assert_eq!(1_u64.wrapping_shl(128), 1);
assert_eq!(5_u64.wrapping_shl(1025), 10);
```

title: u64::wrapping_shr

# u64::wrapping_shr

Kind: method
Defined in: `u64`
Signature: `pub const fn wrapping_shr(self, rhs: u32) -> u64`
Stable since: Rust 1.2.0

Panic-free bitwise shift-right; yields `self >> mask(rhs)`,
where `mask` removes any high-order bits of `rhs` that
would cause the shift to exceed the bitwidth of the type.

Beware that, unlike most other `wrapping_*` methods on integers, this
does *not* give the same result as doing the shift in infinite precision
then truncating as needed. Instead, the behaviour of this method matches what shift instructions
do on many processors, and is what the `>>` operator does when overflow
checks are disabled, but numerically it's weird.  Consider, instead,
using `Self::unbounded_shr` which has nicer behaviour.

Note that this is *not* the same as a rotate-right; the
RHS of a wrapping shift-right is restricted to the range
of the type, rather than the bits shifted out of the LHS
being returned to the other end. The primitive integer
types all implement a `rotate_right` function,
which may be what you want instead.

# Examples

```rust
assert_eq!(128_u64.wrapping_shr(7), 1);
assert_eq!(0b1010_u64.wrapping_shr(0), 0b1010);
assert_eq!(0b1010_u64.wrapping_shr(1), 0b101);
assert_eq!(0b1010_u64.wrapping_shr(2), 0b10);
assert_eq!(u64::MAX.wrapping_shr(1), i64::MAX.cast_unsigned());
assert_eq!(42_u64.wrapping_shr(64), 42);
assert_eq!(42_u64.wrapping_shr(1).wrapping_shr(63), 0);
assert_eq!(128_u64.wrapping_shr(128), 128);
assert_eq!(10_u64.wrapping_shr(1025), 5);
```

# u8::from_be

Kind: method
Defined in: `u8`
Signature: `pub const fn from_be(x: u8) -> u8`
Stable since: Rust 1.0.0

Converts an integer from big endian to the target's endianness.

On big endian this is a no-op. On little endian the bytes are
swapped.

# Examples

```rust
let n = 0x1Au8;

if cfg!(target_endian = "big") {
    assert_eq!(u8::from_be(n), n)
} else {
    assert_eq!(u8::from_be(n), n.swap_bytes())
}
```

title: u8::from_be_bytes
text:
# u8::from_be_bytes

Kind: method
Defined in: `u8`
Signature: `pub const fn from_be_bytes(bytes: [u8; 1]) -> u8`
Stable since: Rust 1.32.0

Creates a native endian integer value from its representation
as a byte array in big endian.

**Note**: This function is meaningless on `u8`. Byte order does not exist as a
concept for byte-sized integers. This function is only provided in symmetry
with larger integer types.

# Examples

```rust
let value = u8::from_be_bytes([0x12]);
assert_eq!(value, 0x12);
```

When starting from a slice rather than an array, fallible conversion APIs can be used:

```rust
fn read_be_u8(input: &mut &[u8]) -> u8 {
    let (int_bytes, rest) = input.split_at(size_of::<u8>());
    *input = rest;
    u8::from_be_bytes(int_bytes.try_into().unwrap())
}
```

# u8::from_str_radix

Kind: method
Defined in: `u8`
Signature: `pub const fn from_str_radix(src: &str, radix: u32) -> Result<u8, ParseIntError>`
Stable since: Rust 1.0.0

Parses an integer from a string slice with digits in a given base.

The string is expected to be an optional
 `+` 
sign followed by only digits. Leading and trailing non-digit characters (including
whitespace) represent an error. Underscores (which are accepted in Rust literals)
also represent an error.

Digits are a subset of these characters, depending on `radix`:
* `0-9`
* `a-z`
* `A-Z`

# Panics

This function panics if `radix` is not in the range from 2 to 36.

# See also
If the string to be parsed is in base 10 (decimal),
`from_str` or `str::parse` can also be used.

# Examples

```rust
assert_eq!(u8::from_str_radix("A", 16), Ok(10));
```
Trailing space returns error:
```rust
assert!(u8::from_str_radix("1 ", 10).is_err());
```

Stable since: Rust 1.7.0

Calculates the multiplication of `self` and `rhs`.

Returns a tuple of the multiplication along with a boolean
indicating whether an arithmetic overflow would occur. If an
overflow would have occurred then the wrapped value is returned.

If you want the *value* of the overflow, rather than just *whether*
an overflow occurred, see `Self::carrying_mul`.

Please note that this example is shared among integer types, which is why `u32` is used.

not overflow.

Kind: method
Defined in: `u8`
Signature: `pub const fn overflowing_shl(self, rhs: u32) -> (u8, bool)`
Stable since: Rust 1.7.0

Shifts self left by `rhs` bits.

Returns a tuple of the shifted version of self along with a boolean
indicating whether the shift value was larger than or equal to the
number of bits. If the shift value is too large, then value is
masked (N-1) where N is the number of bits, and this value is then
used to perform the shift.


title: u8::rotate_left
text:
# u8::rotate_left

Kind: method
Defined in: `u8`
Signature: `pub const fn rotate_left(self, n: u32) -> u8`
Stable since: Rust 1.0.0

Shifts the bits to the left by a specified amount, `n`,
wrapping the truncated bits to the end of the resulting integer.

`rotate_left(n)` is equivalent to applying `rotate_left(1)` a total of `n` times. In
particular, a rotation by the number of bits in `self` returns the input value
unchanged.

Please note this isn't the same operation as the `<<` shifting operator!

# Examples

```rust
let n = 0x82u8;
let m = 0x0a;

assert_eq!(n.rotate_left(2), m);
assert_eq!(n.rotate_left(1024), n);
```

wrapping the truncated bits to the beginning of the resulting
integer.

`rotate_right(n)` is equivalent to applying `rotate_right(1)` a total of `n` times. In
particular, a rotation by the number of bits in `self` returns the input value
unchanged.

Please note this isn't the same operation as the `>>` shifting operator!

# Examples

```rust

let m = 0x82;

assert_eq!(n.rotate_right(2), m);
assert_eq!(n.rotate_right(1024), n);
```

Kind: method
Defined in: `u8`
Signature: `pub const fn strict_add(self, rhs: u8) -> u8`
Stable since: Rust 1.91.0

Strict integer addition. Computes `self + rhs`, panicking
if overflow occurred.

This function will always panic on overflow, regardless of whether overflow checks are enabled.

# Examples


Signature: `pub const fn to_be_bytes(self) -> [u8; 1]`
Stable since: Rust 1.32.0

Returns the memory representation of this integer as a byte array in
big-endian (network) byte order.

**Note**: This function is meaningless on `u8`. Byte order does not exist as a
concept for byte-sized integers. This function is only provided in symmetry
with larger integer types.

# Examples

```rust
let bytes = 0x12u8.to_be_bytes();
assert_eq!(bytes, [0x12]);
```

title: u8::to_le

# u8::to_le

Kind: method
Defined in: `u8`
Signature: `pub const fn to_le(self) -> u8`
Stable since: Rust 1.0.0

Converts `self` to little endian from the target's endianness.

On little endian this is a no-op. On big endian the bytes are
swapped.

# Examples

```rust
let n = 0x1Au8;

if cfg!(target_endian = "little") {
    assert_eq!(n.to_le(), n)
} else {
    assert_eq!(n.to_le(), n.swap_bytes())
}
```

# u8::to_ne_bytes

Kind: method
Defined in: `u8`
Signature: `pub const fn to_ne_bytes(self) -> [u8; 1]`
Stable since: Rust 1.32.0

Returns the memory representation of this integer as a byte array in
native byte order.

As the target platform's native endianness is used, portable code
should use `to_be_bytes` or `to_le_bytes`, as appropriate,
instead.

**Note**: This function is meaningless on `u8`. Byte order does not exist as a
concept for byte-sized integers. This function is only provided in symmetry
with larger integer types.

# Examples

```rust
let bytes = 0x12u8.to_ne_bytes();
assert_eq!(
    bytes,
    if cfg!(target_endian = "big") {
        [0x12]
    } else {
        [0x12]
    }
);
```

# u8::unchecked_add

Kind: method
Defined in: `u8`
Signature: `pub const unsafe fn unchecked_add(self, rhs: u8) -> u8`
Stable since: Rust 1.79.0

Unchecked integer addition. Computes `self + rhs`, assuming overflow

Calling `x.unchecked_add(y)` is semantically equivalent to calling
`x.``checked_add``(y).``unwrap_unchecked``()`.

If you're just trying to avoid the panic in debug mode, then **do not**

title: u8::unchecked_sub

# u8::unchecked_sub

Kind: method
Defined in: `u8`
Signature: `pub const unsafe fn unchecked_sub(self, rhs: u8) -> u8`
Stable since: Rust 1.79.0

Unchecked integer subtraction. Computes `self - rhs`, assuming overflow
cannot occur.

Calling `x.unchecked_sub(y)` is semantically equivalent to calling
`x.``checked_sub``(y).``unwrap_unchecked``()`.

If you're just trying to avoid the panic in debug mode, then **do not**
use this.  Instead, you're looking for `wrapping_sub`.

If you find yourself writing code like this:

```rust
if foo >= bar {
    // SAFETY: just checked it will not overflow
    let diff = unsafe { foo.unchecked_sub(bar) };
    // ... use diff ...
}
```

Consider changing it to

```rust
if let Some(diff) = foo.checked_sub(bar) {
    // ... use diff ...
}
```

As that does exactly the same thing -- including telling the optimizer
that the subtraction cannot overflow -- but avoids needing `unsafe`.

# Safety

This results in undefined behavior when overflow occurs, i.e. when
`checked_sub` would return `None`.

# u8::wrapping_div

Kind: method
Defined in: `u8`
Signature: `pub const fn wrapping_div(self, rhs: u8) -> u8`
Stable since: Rust 1.2.0

Wrapping (modular) division. Computes `self / rhs`.

Wrapped division on unsigned types is just normal division. There's
no way wrapping could ever happen. This function exists so that all
operations are accounted for in the wrapping operations.

title: u8::wrapping_neg
text:
# u8::wrapping_neg

Kind: method
Defined in: `u8`
Signature: `pub const fn wrapping_neg(self) -> u8`
Stable since: Rust 1.2.0

Wrapping (modular) negation. Computes `-self`,
wrapping around at the boundary of the type.

Since unsigned types do not have negative equivalents
all applications of this function will wrap (except for `-0`).
For values smaller than the corresponding signed type's maximum
the result is the same as casting the corresponding signed value.
Any larger values are equivalent to `MAX + 1 - (val - MAX - 1)` where
`MAX` is the corresponding signed type's maximum.

# Examples

```rust
assert_eq!(0_u8.wrapping_neg(), 0);
assert_eq!(u8::MAX.wrapping_neg(), 1);
assert_eq!(13_u8.wrapping_neg(), (!13) + 1);
assert_eq!(42_u8.wrapping_neg(), !(42 - 1));
```

title: u8::wrapping_shl
text:
# u8::wrapping_shl

Kind: method
Defined in: `u8`
Signature: `pub const fn wrapping_shl(self, rhs: u32) -> u8`
Stable since: Rust 1.2.0

Panic-free bitwise shift-left; yields `self << mask(rhs)`,
where `mask` removes any high-order bits of `rhs` that
would cause the shift to exceed the bitwidth of the type.

Beware that, unlike most other `wrapping_*` methods on integers, this
does *not* give the same result as doing the shift in infinite precision
then truncating as needed. Instead, the behaviour of this method matches what shift instructions
do on many processors, and is what the `<<` operator does when overflow
checks are disabled, but numerically it's weird.  Consider, instead,
using `Self::unbounded_shl` which has nicer behaviour.

Note that this is *not* the same as a rotate-left; the
RHS of a wrapping shift-left is restricted to the range
of the type, rather than the bits shifted out of the LHS
being returned to the other end. The primitive integer
types all implement a `rotate_left` function,
which may be what you want instead.

# Examples

```rust
assert_eq!(1_u8.wrapping_shl(7), 128);
assert_eq!(0b101_u8.wrapping_shl(0), 0b101);
assert_eq!(0b101_u8.wrapping_shl(1), 0b1010);
assert_eq!(0b101_u8.wrapping_shl(2), 0b10100);
assert_eq!(u8::MAX.wrapping_shl(2), u8::MAX - 3);
assert_eq!(42_u8.wrapping_shl(8), 42);
assert_eq!(42_u8.wrapping_shl(1).wrapping_shl(7), 0);
assert_eq!(1_u8.wrapping_shl(128), 1);
assert_eq!(5_u8.wrapping_shl(1025), 10);
```

title: u8::wrapping_shr

# u8::wrapping_shr

Kind: method
Defined in: `u8`
Signature: `pub const fn wrapping_shr(self, rhs: u32) -> u8`
Stable since: Rust 1.2.0

Panic-free bitwise shift-right; yields `self >> mask(rhs)`,
where `mask` removes any high-order bits of `rhs` that
would cause the shift to exceed the bitwidth of the type.

Beware that, unlike most other `wrapping_*` methods on integers, this
does *not* give the same result as doing the shift in infinite precision
then truncating as needed. Instead, the behaviour of this method matches what shift instructions
do on many processors, and is what the `>>` operator does when overflow
checks are disabled, but numerically it's weird.  Consider, instead,
using `Self::unbounded_shr` which has nicer behaviour.

Note that this is *not* the same as a rotate-right; the
RHS of a wrapping shift-right is restricted to the range
of the type, rather than the bits shifted out of the LHS
being returned to the other end. The primitive integer
types all implement a `rotate_right` function,
which may be what you want instead.

# Examples

```rust
assert_eq!(128_u8.wrapping_shr(7), 1);
assert_eq!(0b1010_u8.wrapping_shr(0), 0b1010);
assert_eq!(0b1010_u8.wrapping_shr(1), 0b101);
assert_eq!(0b1010_u8.wrapping_shr(2), 0b10);
assert_eq!(u8::MAX.wrapping_shr(1), i8::MAX.cast_unsigned());
assert_eq!(42_u8.wrapping_shr(8), 42);
assert_eq!(42_u8.wrapping_shr(1).wrapping_shr(7), 0);
assert_eq!(128_u8.wrapping_shr(128), 128);
assert_eq!(10_u8.wrapping_shr(1025), 5);
```

Kind: associated constant

# usize::from_be

Kind: method
Defined in: `usize`
Signature: `pub const fn from_be(x: usize) -> usize`
Stable since: Rust 1.0.0

Converts an integer from big endian to the target's endianness.

On big endian this is a no-op. On little endian the bytes are
swapped.

# Examples

```rust
let n = 0x1Ausize;

if cfg!(target_endian = "big") {
    assert_eq!(usize::from_be(n), n)
} else {
    assert_eq!(usize::from_be(n), n.swap_bytes())
}
```

title: usize::from_be_bytes
text:
# usize::from_be_bytes

Kind: method
Defined in: `usize`
Signature: `pub const fn from_be_bytes(bytes: [u8; 8]) -> usize`
Stable since: Rust 1.32.0

Creates a native endian integer value from its representation
as a byte array in big endian.

**Note**: This function takes an array of length 2, 4 or 8 bytes
depending on the target pointer size.

# Examples

```rust
let value = usize::from_be_bytes([0x12, 0x34, 0x56, 0x78, 0x90, 0x12, 0x34, 0x56]);
assert_eq!(value, 0x1234567890123456);
```

When starting from a slice rather than an array, fallible conversion APIs can be used:

```rust
fn read_be_usize(input: &mut &[u8]) -> usize {
    let (int_bytes, rest) = input.split_at(size_of::<usize>());
    *input = rest;
    usize::from_be_bytes(int_bytes.try_into().unwrap())
}
```

# usize::from_str_radix

Kind: method
Defined in: `usize`
Signature: `pub const fn from_str_radix(src: &str, radix: u32) -> Result<usize, ParseIntError>`
Stable since: Rust 1.0.0

Parses an integer from a string slice with digits in a given base.

The string is expected to be an optional
 `+` 
sign followed by only digits. Leading and trailing non-digit characters (including
whitespace) represent an error. Underscores (which are accepted in Rust literals)
also represent an error.

Digits are a subset of these characters, depending on `radix`:
* `0-9`
* `a-z`
* `A-Z`

# Panics

This function panics if `radix` is not in the range from 2 to 36.

# See also
If the string to be parsed is in base 10 (decimal),
`from_str` or `str::parse` can also be used.

# Examples

```rust
assert_eq!(usize::from_str_radix("A", 16), Ok(10));
```
Trailing space returns error:
```rust
assert!(usize::from_str_radix("1 ", 10).is_err());
```

Kind: method

Stable since: Rust 1.7.0

Calculates the divisor when `self` is divided by `rhs`.

whether an arithmetic overflow would occur. Note that for unsigned

# Panics


title: usize::rotate_left
text:
# usize::rotate_left

Kind: method
Defined in: `usize`
Signature: `pub const fn rotate_left(self, n: u32) -> usize`
Stable since: Rust 1.0.0

Shifts the bits to the left by a specified amount, `n`,
wrapping the truncated bits to the end of the resulting integer.

`rotate_left(n)` is equivalent to applying `rotate_left(1)` a total of `n` times. In
particular, a rotation by the number of bits in `self` returns the input value
unchanged.

Please note this isn't the same operation as the `<<` shifting operator!

# Examples

```rust
let n = 0x0aa00000000006e1usize;
let m = 0x00000000006e10aa;

assert_eq!(n.rotate_left(12), m);
assert_eq!(n.rotate_left(1024), n);
```

title: usize::rotate_right
text:
# usize::rotate_right

Kind: method
Defined in: `usize`
Signature: `pub const fn rotate_right(self, n: u32) -> usize`
Stable since: Rust 1.0.0

Shifts the bits to the right by a specified amount, `n`,
wrapping the truncated bits to the beginning of the resulting
integer.

`rotate_right(n)` is equivalent to applying `rotate_right(1)` a total of `n` times. In
particular, a rotation by the number of bits in `self` returns the input value
unchanged.

Please note this isn't the same operation as the `>>` shifting operator!

# Examples

```rust
let n = 0x00000000006e10aausize;
let m = 0x0aa00000000006e1;

assert_eq!(n.rotate_right(12), m);
assert_eq!(n.rotate_right(1024), n);
```

# usize::to_be

Kind: method
Defined in: `usize`
Signature: `pub const fn to_be(self) -> usize`
Stable since: Rust 1.0.0

Converts `self` to big endian from the target's endianness.

On big endian this is a no-op. On little endian the bytes are
swapped.

# Examples

```rust
let n = 0x1Ausize;

    assert_eq!(n.to_be(), n)
} else {
    assert_eq!(n.to_be(), n.swap_bytes())
}
```

depending on the target pointer size.

# Examples

```rust
let bytes = 0x1234567890123456usize.to_le_bytes();
assert_eq!(bytes, [0x56, 0x34, 0x12, 0x90, 0x78, 0x56, 0x34, 0x12]);
```

# usize::to_ne_bytes

Kind: method
Defined in: `usize`
Signature: `pub const fn to_ne_bytes(self) -> [u8; 8]`
Stable since: Rust 1.32.0

Returns the memory representation of this integer as a byte array in
native byte order.

As the target platform's native endianness is used, portable code
should use `to_be_bytes` or `to_le_bytes`, as appropriate,
instead.

**Note**: This function returns an array of length 2, 4 or 8 bytes
depending on the target pointer size.

# Examples

```rust
let bytes = 0x1234567890123456usize.to_ne_bytes();
assert_eq!(
    bytes,
    if cfg!(target_endian = "big") {
        [0x12, 0x34, 0x56, 0x78, 0x90, 0x12, 0x34, 0x56]
    } else {
        [0x56, 0x34, 0x12, 0x90, 0x78, 0x56, 0x34, 0x12]
    }
);
```

# usize::unchecked_add

Kind: method
Defined in: `usize`
Signature: `pub const unsafe fn unchecked_add(self, rhs: usize) -> usize`
Stable since: Rust 1.79.0

Unchecked integer addition. Computes `self + rhs`, assuming overflow
cannot occur.

Calling `x.unchecked_add(y)` is semantically equivalent to calling
`x.``checked_add``(y).``unwrap_unchecked``()`.

If you're just trying to avoid the panic in debug mode, then **do not**
use this.  Instead, you're looking for `wrapping_add`.

# Safety

This results in undefined behavior when overflow occurs, i.e. when

# usize::unchecked_sub

Kind: method
Defined in: `usize`
Signature: `pub const unsafe fn unchecked_sub(self, rhs: usize) -> usize`
Stable since: Rust 1.79.0

Unchecked integer subtraction. Computes `self - rhs`, assuming overflow
cannot occur.

Calling `x.unchecked_sub(y)` is semantically equivalent to calling
`x.``checked_sub``(y).``unwrap_unchecked``()`.

If you're just trying to avoid the panic in debug mode, then **do not**
use this.  Instead, you're looking for `wrapping_sub`.

If you find yourself writing code like this:

```rust
if foo >= bar {
    // SAFETY: just checked it will not overflow
    let diff = unsafe { foo.unchecked_sub(bar) };
    // ... use diff ...
}
```

Consider changing it to

```rust
if let Some(diff) = foo.checked_sub(bar) {
    // ... use diff ...
}
```

As that does exactly the same thing -- including telling the optimizer
that the subtraction cannot overflow -- but avoids needing `unsafe`.

# Safety

This results in undefined behavior when overflow occurs, i.e. when
`checked_sub` would return `None`.

# usize::wrapping_div

Kind: method
Defined in: `usize`
Signature: `pub const fn wrapping_div(self, rhs: usize) -> usize`
Stable since: Rust 1.2.0

Wrapping (modular) division. Computes `self / rhs`.

Wrapped division on unsigned types is just normal division. There's
no way wrapping could ever happen. This function exists so that all
operations are accounted for in the wrapping operations.

# Panics

This function will panic if `rhs` is zero.

# Examples

```rust
assert_eq!(100usize.wrapping_div(10), 10);
```

title: usize::wrapping_neg
text:
# usize::wrapping_neg

Kind: method
Defined in: `usize`
Signature: `pub const fn wrapping_neg(self) -> usize`
Stable since: Rust 1.2.0

Wrapping (modular) negation. Computes `-self`,
wrapping around at the boundary of the type.

Since unsigned types do not have negative equivalents
all applications of this function will wrap (except for `-0`).
For values smaller than the corresponding signed type's maximum
the result is the same as casting the corresponding signed value.
Any larger values are equivalent to `MAX + 1 - (val - MAX - 1)` where
`MAX` is the corresponding signed type's maximum.

# Examples

```rust
assert_eq!(0_usize.wrapping_neg(), 0);
assert_eq!(usize::MAX.wrapping_neg(), 1);
assert_eq!(13_usize.wrapping_neg(), (!13) + 1);
assert_eq!(42_usize.wrapping_neg(), !(42 - 1));
```

title: usize::wrapping_shl
text:
# usize::wrapping_shl

Kind: method
Defined in: `usize`
Signature: `pub const fn wrapping_shl(self, rhs: u32) -> usize`
Stable since: Rust 1.2.0

Panic-free bitwise shift-left; yields `self << mask(rhs)`,
where `mask` removes any high-order bits of `rhs` that
would cause the shift to exceed the bitwidth of the type.

Beware that, unlike most other `wrapping_*` methods on integers, this
does *not* give the same result as doing the shift in infinite precision
then truncating as needed. Instead, the behaviour of this method matches what shift instructions
do on many processors, and is what the `<<` operator does when overflow
checks are disabled, but numerically it's weird.  Consider, instead,
using `Self::unbounded_shl` which has nicer behaviour.

Note that this is *not* the same as a rotate-left; the
RHS of a wrapping shift-left is restricted to the range
of the type, rather than the bits shifted out of the LHS
being returned to the other end. The primitive integer
types all implement a `rotate_left` function,
which may be what you want instead.

# Examples

```rust
assert_eq!(1_usize.wrapping_shl(7), 128);
assert_eq!(0b101_usize.wrapping_shl(0), 0b101);
assert_eq!(0b101_usize.wrapping_shl(1), 0b1010);
assert_eq!(0b101_usize.wrapping_shl(2), 0b10100);
assert_eq!(usize::MAX.wrapping_shl(2), usize::MAX - 3);
assert_eq!(42_usize.wrapping_shl(64), 42);
assert_eq!(42_usize.wrapping_shl(1).wrapping_shl(63), 0);
assert_eq!(1_usize.wrapping_shl(128), 1);
assert_eq!(5_usize.wrapping_shl(1025), 10);
```

title: usize::wrapping_shr
text:
# usize::wrapping_shr

Kind: method
Defined in: `usize`
Signature: `pub const fn wrapping_shr(self, rhs: u32) -> usize`
Stable since: Rust 1.2.0

Panic-free bitwise shift-right; yields `self >> mask(rhs)`,
where `mask` removes any high-order bits of `rhs` that
would cause the shift to exceed the bitwidth of the type.

Beware that, unlike most other `wrapping_*` methods on integers, this
does *not* give the same result as doing the shift in infinite precision
then truncating as needed. Instead, the behaviour of this method matches what shift instructions
do on many processors, and is what the `>>` operator does when overflow
checks are disabled, but numerically it's weird.  Consider, instead,
using `Self::unbounded_shr` which has nicer behaviour.

Note that this is *not* the same as a rotate-right; the
RHS of a wrapping shift-right is restricted to the range
of the type, rather than the bits shifted out of the LHS
being returned to the other end. The primitive integer
types all implement a `rotate_right` function,
which may be what you want instead.

# Examples

```rust
assert_eq!(128_usize.wrapping_shr(7), 1);
assert_eq!(0b1010_usize.wrapping_shr(0), 0b1010);
assert_eq!(0b1010_usize.wrapping_shr(1), 0b101);
assert_eq!(0b1010_usize.wrapping_shr(2), 0b10);
assert_eq!(usize::MAX.wrapping_shr(1), isize::MAX.cast_unsigned());
assert_eq!(42_usize.wrapping_shr(64), 42);
assert_eq!(42_usize.wrapping_shr(1).wrapping_shr(63), 0);
assert_eq!(128_usize.wrapping_shr(128), 128);
assert_eq!(10_usize.wrapping_shr(1025), 5);
```
